guides.title: Marks on Stone: Global Wall & Rock Art in Toto
guides.description: Comparative illustrated archive across every inhabited continent—from monumental Paleolithic caves like Lascaux and Sulawesi to desert rock overhangs in Nevada, the Sahara, Australia and Patagonia.
guides.intro: Before cities or alphabets, human communities painted mineral pigments inside limestone caverns, pecked desert-varnished boulders beside waterholes, scraped colossal earth figures into alluvial terraces, and sheltered modest stories beneath wind-carved rock overhangs. Brought together in toto, these visual records reveal shared human creativity shaped by radically different environments.
guides.scope: Spans >51,000 years globally using direct radiocarbon, OSL luminescence, U-series carbonate crusts, and living Indigenous knowledge. All rock-art ages remain approximate minimum or bracketed windows.

sections.heading: Two Extremes on Stone: Deep Dark Caves vs. Sunlit Desert Overhangs

paragraphs.text: Deep limestone cathedral caves like Lascaux and Chauvet in France—or the pitch-black Mississippi and Tennessee passages of Picture Cave and Mud Glyph Cave—demanded stone lamps or rivercane torches, ochre palettes and collective ritual isolation far underground. Yet across most of human history and geography, the dominant studio was far more intimate: shallow rock overhangs, sun-warmed granite shelves, or basalt boulders beside desert springs in Nevada, California, Nubia, the Sahara, Central India and Patagonia.

In Nevada alone, small volcanic tuff alcoves like Toquima Cave, coastal Lake Lahontan tufa ledges at Winnemucca Lake, and wind-scooped Aztec sandstone niches in Valley of Fire or Sloan Canyon preserve fragile geometric rings, rakes, bighorn sheep and handprints made within steps of open-air family campfires and pinyon trails. Placing Lascaux and Toquima Cave side by side in toto reveals that monumentality never measured cultural depth: small desert overhangs sustained continuous visual traditions every bit as durable as subterranean European sanctuaries.

sections.heading: How Rock Art Is Dated (and Why Dates Remain Approximate)

paragraphs.text: Carved lines on stone and mineral-iron red ochres contain no organic carbon of their own, so archaeologists combine multiple indirect and direct clocks: uranium-series dating of mineral calcite skins grown over paint in Sulawesi (~51.2 ka); optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) of windblown sand burying petroglyphs at Qurta (>15 ka) and rockfall below Utah's Great Gallery (~1–1100 CE); plasma-chemical oxidation AMS dating of plant/fat binders in Lower Pecos paint (~3700 BCE–900 CE); radiocarbon on Lake Lahontan carbonate crusts sealing Winnemucca Lake incisions (~14.8–10.5 cal ka); and direct AMS charcoal dating inside Chauvet and Missouri's Picture Cave.

cells: Natural ochre stencils & scene in karst cave

paragraphs.text: Rock walls remain sacred archives for descendant Indigenous communities worldwide—among Bininj/Mungguy, Ngarinyin, San, Chewa, Niitsítapi, Anishinaabe, Hopi, Pueblo, Paiute, Shoshone and Chumash stewards. Touching pigments, chalking engravings, or building unmonitored fires permanently destroys microscopic binders needed both for cultural preservation and scientific dating.

guides.title: Pictographs, Petroglyphs & Painted Caves of North America
guides.description: Continental survey linking >70 North American rock-art complexes—from Winnemucca Lake and Nevada desert overhangs to Lower Pecos murals, Canadian Shield cliffs and Eastern dark-zone caves—to their Indigenous cultures.
guides.intro: Across every physiographic zone of North America, Indigenous peoples left dense visual histories etched into volcanic basalt, painted beneath high sandstone alcoves, modeled into deep pitch-black cave mud, and scraped into desert gravels. Far from anonymous scratches, these sites connect directly to Numic, Puebloan, Fremont, Cochimí, Olmec, Maya, Niitsítapi, Anishinaabe, Cherokee, Makah, Tlingit and Mississippian traditions.
guides.scope: Catalogs 71 map-pinned sites across 8 regions using approximate archaeological intervals (Benson et al., Steelman et al., Pederson et al., Diaz-Granados et al., Simek et al., NPS, BLM and UNESCO dossiers).

paragraphs.text: Starting along receding Lake Lahontan shorelines at Winnemucca Lake (~14,800–10,500 cal BP) and continuing through Grimes Point, Toquima Cave, Lagomarsino Canyon, Hickison Summit, Pahranagat Valley, Sloan Canyon, Valley of Fire and Gold Butte, Great Basin artists used intimate volcanic tuff overhangs, basalt talus ridges and Aztec sandstone seams overlooking scarce mountain springs.

sections.heading: Regional Styles from Baja Caverns to Dark-Zone Caves

paragraphs.text: Farther east and south, artists shifted media dramatically with geology: glowing polychrome hematite, gypsum and black mineral paint across Chumash, Lower Pecos and Baja California canyon overhangs; monumental earth-scraped intaglios along Lower Colorado desert terraces; red iron-oxide Mishipeshu cliffs painted from canoes across the Canadian Shield; and deep underground Mississippian clay drawings lit solely by burning rivercane torches in Tennessee, Missouri and Alabama karst.

In the main #explore map (filterable under 'Rock art & visual records'), all 71 newly added North American rock-art entries carry explicit attribution to their documented Indigenous makers and heritage traditions while honestly retaining approximate intervals.
